Discovering how those adaptations

make us more vulnerable to certain
diseases is an important facet of
evolutionary medicine, an emerging
specialty that views health through the

lens of evolutionary theory. This
approach sheds light on many common

ailments that have arisen.

For comparison, non-athletes have only a
5 to 10 per cent difference. This finding
suggests that we retain our ancient
capacity for strength. In turn, stronger
bones mean fewer fractures. Broken hips,
for example, were less common in the
past and are rare in archaeological
specimens, even accounting for the fact
that lives were shorter.

There are other physical changes.
Some of us seem to have acquired a new

median artery. In fact, this blood vessel is
present in the embryo but it normally
vanishes around the eighth week of
pregnancy, to be replaced by the ulnar
and radial arteries. An increasing number
of adults now retain this artery, up from
10 per cent at the beginning of the 20th
century to 30 per cent at the end. Ruhli’s
former teacher, Maciej Henneberg, is
helping document this change. It could be
due to differences in the diet of pregnant
mothers, he speculates, or modern
medicine.

It is this kind of uncertainty that leaves
some doctors unimpressed with
evolutionary medicine. We cannot know if
evolutionary explanations are true, since
we rarely have a complete picture of the
past, points out American family
physician Harriet Hall. ‘Conventional
medicine has a long record of successes,’
she says. ‘Evolutionary medicine hasn't
proven it has any real value.’ That's not
to say that documenting trends over time
